etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English murmur, murmor, murmour, from Old French murmure (modern French murmure), from Latin murmur (“murmur, humming, muttering, roaring, growling, rushing etc.”).

definitions.definition: (countable, uncountable) Any low, indistinct sound, like that of running water.

quote.citation: 1854, Narrative of a Journey Round the Dead Sea, and in the Bible Lands:
quote.text: The delightful murmur of water running over pebbles is heard a few yards off

quote.citation: 1979: A translation of the Eclogues by Paul Alpers
quote.text: The windy murmur of the breeze subsides.

quote.citation: 1874, Marcus Clarke, chapter V, in For the Term of His Natural Life:
quote.text: In the prison of the 'tween decks reigned a darkness pregnant with murmurs. The sentry at the entrance to the hatchway was supposed to "prevent the prisoners from making a noise," but he put a very liberal interpretation upon the clause, and so long as the prisoners refrained from shouting, yelling, and fighting--eccentricities in which they sometimes indulged--he did not disturb them.

quote.citation: 1960, P. G. Wodehouse, chapter XI, in Jeeves in the Offing:
quote.text: The moment had come for the honeyed word. I lowered my voice to a confidential murmur, but on her inquiring if I had laryngitis raised it again.

definitions.definition: (cardiology, medicine) The sound made by any condition which produces noisy, or turbulent, flow of blood through the heart.
A muttered complaint or protest; the expression of dissatisfaction in a low muttering voice; any expression of complaint or discontent.

quote.citation: 1919, Boris Sidis, The Source and Aim of Human Progress:
quote.text: In fear of disease and in the interest of his health man will be muzzled and masked like a vicious dog, and that without any murmur of complaint.

quote.citation: 2004, Euan A. Ashley, Josef Niebauer, Cardiology Explained:
quote.text: Since aortic diastolic pressure is higher than pulmonary artery systolic pressure, there is continuous flow into the pulmonary circulation, creating the characteristic continuous ("machinery") murmur, heard best just below the left clavicle.

quote.citation: 1960, P. G. Wodehouse, chapter XX, in Jeeves in the Offing:
quote.text: Glossop will return from his afternoon off to find the awful majesty of the Law waiting for him, complete with handcuffs. We can hardly expect him to accept an exemplary sentence without a murmur, so his first move will be to establish his innocence by revealing all.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, now rare) To grumble; to complain in a low, muttering voice, or express discontent at or against someone or something. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, John vj:[41]:
quote.text: The Iewes then murmured at him because he sayde: I am that breed which is come doune from heaven.
And now, behold thy brothers murmur, saying it is a hard thing which I have required of them; but behold I have not required it of them, but it is a commandment of the Lord.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To speak or make low, indistinguishable noise; to mumble, mutter. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1921, Ben Travers, chapter 7, in A Cuckoo in the Nest, Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday, Page & Company, published 1925, →OCLC:
quote.text: “Oh yes,” he murmured in a tone of obligatory surprise, as he proceeded to make the kind of 2 which he attributed to Margaret's style of chirography.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To say (something) indistinctly, to mutter. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii], line 51:
quote.text: I  […]  heard thee murmur tales of iron wars;

quote.citation: 1874, Thomas Hardy, chapter 21, in Far from the Madding Crowd. […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: Smith, Elder & Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Gabriel murmured a confused reply, and hastened on.

quote.citation: 1942, Lloyd C. Douglas, chapter 7, in The Robe‎[1]:
quote.text: With a husky voice she murmured that he was the very dearest grandfather anyone ever had.

quote.citation: 1978, Andrew Holleran, chapter 4, in Dancer from the Dance‎[2], New York: New American Library, published 1986, page 105:
quote.text: “ […]  Don’t look now,” he murmured, lowering his eyes demurely, “but the most handsome man in Brookfield, Connecticut, has just walked in the room.”
